title: Phase Changes
lead: An ideal gas never condenses, but a real gas does when it is cooled or squeezed enough, and it freezes when it is cooled further. This section follows a real gas away from the ideal gas law on two graphs, the PV diagram with its isotherms and its critical point and the phase diagram with its regions, its boundaries and its triple point, explains what it means for a liquid and its gas to be in equilibrium, and ends with vapor pressure, partial pressure and Dalton’s law.
objectives: Identify and describe the triple point of a gas from its phase diagram.
Describe the state of equilibrium between a liquid and a gas, a liquid and a solid, and a gas and a solid.
summary_html:
• Most substances have three distinct phases: gas, liquid, and solid.
  • Phase changes among the various phases of matter depend on temperature and pressure.
  • The existence of the three phases with respect to pressure and temperature can be described in a phase diagram.
  • Two phases coexist (i.e., they are in thermal equilibrium) at a set of pressures and temperatures. These are described as a line on a phase diagram.
  • The three phases coexist at a single pressure and temperature. This is known as the triple point and is described by a single point on a phase diagram.
  • A gas at a temperature below its boiling point is called a vapor.
  • Vapor pressure is the pressure at which a gas coexists with its solid or liquid phase.
  • Partial pressure is the pressure a gas would create if it existed alone.
  • Dalton’s law states that the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of all of the gases present.

figures.original_caption: A sketch of volume versus temperature for a real gas at constant pressure. The linear (straight line) part of the graph represents ideal gas behavior—volume and temperature are directly and positively related and the line extrapolates to zero volume at −273.15 °C, or absolute zero. When the gas becomes a liquid, however, the volume actually decreases precipitously at the liquefaction point. The volume decreases slightly once the substance is solid, but it never becomes zero.

PV diagrams. (a) Each curve (isotherm) represents the relationship between P and V at a fixed temperature; the upper curves are at higher temperatures. The lower curves are not hyperbolas, because the gas is no longer an ideal gas. (b) An expanded portion of the PV diagram for low temperatures, where the phase can change from a gas to a liquid. The term “vapor” refers to the gas phase when it exists at a temperature below the boiling temperature.
The phase diagram (PT graph) for water. Note that the axes are nonlinear and the graph is not to scale. This graph is simplified—there are several other exotic phases of ice at higher pressures.

Equilibrium between liquid and gas at two different boiling points inside a closed container. (a) The rates of boiling and condensation are equal at this combination of temperature and pressure, so the liquid and gas phases are in equilibrium. (b) At a higher temperature, the boiling rate is faster and the rates at which molecules leave the liquid and enter the gas are also faster. Because there are more molecules in the gas, the gas pressure is higher and the rate at which gas molecules condense and enter the liquid is faster. As a result the gas and liquid are in equilibrium at this higher temperature.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a cup of water (or soda) with ice cubes stays at 0 °C, even on a hot summer day.

answer.solution: The ice and liquid water are in thermal equilibrium, so that the temperature stays at the freezing temperature as long as ice remains in the liquid. (Once all of the ice melts, the water temperature will start to rise.)

exercises.prompt: Is energy transfer involved in a phase change? If so, will energy have to be supplied to change phase from solid to liquid and liquid to gas? What about gas to liquid and liquid to solid? Why do they spray the orange trees with water in Florida when the temperatures are near or just below freezing?

answer.solution: Yes, energy transfer is involved in a phase change. We know that atoms and molecules in solids and liquids are bound to each other because we know that force is required to separate them. So in a phase change from solid to liquid and liquid to gas, a force must be exerted, perhaps by collision, to separate atoms and molecules. Force exerted through a distance is work, and energy is needed to do work to go from solid to liquid and liquid to gas. This is intuitively consistent with the need for energy to melt ice or boil water. The converse is also true. Going from gas to liquid or liquid to solid involves atoms and molecules pushing together, doing work and releasing energy.

exercises.prompt: A pressure cooker contains water and steam in equilibrium at a pressure greater than atmospheric pressure. How does this greater pressure increase cooking speed?

answer.solution: Read the boiling curve of the phase diagram for water. At 1.00 atm the liquid and its vapor coexist at 100 °C, and the curve rises steadily to the right, so at a higher pressure they coexist at a higher temperature; at about 2 atm, for example, water boils near 120 °C. Inside a sealed pressure cooker the steam cannot escape, its pressure climbs above atmospheric, and the water stays liquid at a temperature well above 100 °C instead of boiling away. The food is therefore cooked in liquid water that is hotter than any open pot can provide, and the chemical changes that cooking consists of go faster at the higher temperature.

exercises.prompt: Why does condensation form most rapidly on the coldest object in a room—for example, on a glass of ice water?

answer.solution: The air in the room carries water vapor at some partial pressure, the same everywhere in the room. Whether liquid forms on a surface depends on comparing that partial pressure with the vapor pressure of water at the temperature of the surface, and the vapor pressure falls steeply as the temperature falls. On a warm object the vapor pressure of water is higher than the partial pressure of the vapor in the air, so any droplet that forms evaporates again. On the glass of ice water the surface is near 0 °C, where the vapor pressure of water is only about 0.006 atm, well below the partial pressure of water vapor in ordinary room air; there the molecules that strike the surface condense faster than they leave it, and liquid collects. The colder the object, the further its vapor pressure lies below the partial pressure in the air, and the faster the condensation.

figure.alt: The phase diagram (pressure versus temperature graph showing the three phases) for carbon dioxide. The triple point is five point one one atmospheres and negative fifty-six point six degrees Celsius. The critical point is seventy-three atmospheres and thirty-one degrees C. The phase change from solid to vapor at standard pressure of one atmosphere is negative seventy-eight point five degrees C.
figure.caption: The phase diagram for carbon dioxide. The axes are nonlinear, and the graph is not to scale. Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide and has a sublimation temperature of −78.5 °C.

exercises.prompt: What is the vapor pressure of solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) at −78.5 °C?

answer.solution: The vapor pressure of a solid is the pressure at which it coexists with its gas, which is the solid–vapor boundary of the phase diagram. The diagram marks −78.5 °C as the sublimation temperature of carbon dioxide at standard atmospheric pressure, so the boundary passes through 1 atm at that temperature, and the vapor pressure of dry ice at −78.5 °C is 1 atm, about 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. This is why dry ice left in the open at ordinary pressure turns to gas without ever becoming a liquid: its triple point lies at 5.11 atm, above atmospheric pressure.

exercises.prompt: Can carbon dioxide be liquefied at room temperature (20 °C)? If so, how? If not, why not? (See the phase diagram for carbon dioxide.)

answer.solution: Yes. The critical temperature of carbon dioxide is 31.1 °C (Table 13.3), and 20 °C lies below it, so a liquid phase exists at that temperature. On the phase diagram a vertical line at 20 °C crosses the liquid–vapor boundary between the triple point at 5.11 atm and the critical point at 73 atm, at a pressure of roughly 60 atm. Compressing the gas at 20 °C to a pressure above that value carries it across the boundary into the liquid region, which is how carbon dioxide is stored as a liquid in a fire extinguisher at room temperature. Above 31.1 °C no pressure, however large, would do this.

exercises.prompt: Oxygen cannot be liquefied at room temperature by placing it under a large enough pressure to force its molecules together. Explain why this is.

answer.solution: Every substance has a critical temperature above which the liquid phase does not exist at any pressure, and for oxygen it is −118.4 °C (Table 13.3). Room temperature is far above that. Compressing oxygen at 20 °C moves it along an isotherm that lies above the critical isotherm on the PV diagram, and such an isotherm has no flat part: the gas is squeezed to the density of a liquid without ever condensing, because at this temperature the molecules move too fast for their mutual attraction to hold them together as a liquid. To liquefy oxygen it must first be cooled below −118.4 °C, and then a large enough pressure will do it; at atmospheric pressure it becomes a liquid at −183 °C.

exercises.prompt: What is the distinction between gas and vapor?

answer.solution: A vapor is the gas phase of a substance when it exists at a temperature below the substance’s boiling temperature, which is to say below the critical temperature, where the gas can coexist with its liquid or solid and can be condensed by pressure alone. Water vapor in the air at 20 °C is a vapor, since water boils at 100 °C at that pressure. Above the critical temperature the substance is simply a gas: no pressure will liquefy it and it cannot coexist with a liquid, as oxygen cannot at room temperature.

exercises.prompt: Dry air is 78.1% nitrogen. What is the partial pressure of nitrogen when the atmospheric pressure is $1.01 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/m}^2$?

answer.hint: By Dalton’s law each gas contributes the pressure it would make alone, and by the ideal gas law that pressure is proportional to its number of molecules. The partial pressure of nitrogen is therefore its fraction of the molecules times the total pressure.

exercises.prompt: A deep-sea diver should breathe a gas mixture that has the same oxygen partial pressure as at sea level, where dry air contains 20.9% oxygen and has a total pressure of $1.01 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/m}^2$. (a) What is the partial pressure of oxygen at sea level? (b) If the diver breathes a gas mixture at a pressure of $2.00 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$, what percent oxygen should it be to have the same oxygen partial pressure as at sea level?

parts.hint: The partial pressure of oxygen is its fraction of the molecules times the total pressure.
The mixture must give the same partial pressure of oxygen at a total pressure about twenty times greater, so the fraction of oxygen must be about twenty times smaller.
